title: True are His devotees
hook: those who live in truth become true (Sukhmani 17)

segments.voice: Yesterday, dargah, and your line: true all through. Were you true in one small thing nobody checks? It's the end of a week that went from no form, no color, to beyond the moods, known by grace, formless everywhere, true then true now, and true all through. Today: what truth does to people. Day five hundred four.

Spend a summer with someone who has a strong accent and you'll come home with a little of it. Live with a person who's always on time and you start, grudgingly, to be on time. We take on the shape of what we're near. Parents notice it with their kids' friends; managers notice it with teams. Gurbani has an old picture for this, about a stone and a piece of iron. And the seventeenth ashtpadi has a line that points the same way. Today: true are His devotees.
screen: `A SUMMER, AND YOU COME HOME WITH AN ACCENT.` → `WE TAKE THE SHAPE OF WHAT WE'RE NEAR.` → `A STONE AND A PIECE OF IRON.`

segments.voice: Go back to yesterday's stanza and look at its pattern again. Every line had two halves. True are His feet, and true is the one who touches them. True His worship, and true the one who serves. True the Name, and true the one who remembers it. The second half is always a person. The stanza ends, in paraphrase: for the one who understands, everything becomes true. So the truth doesn't stay with God. It spreads to whoever comes near it. The devotee, the bhagat, isn't true because they were born that way, or because they're clever about truth. They become true by touching what's true, again and again. Gurbani's picture for this is the paras, the philosopher's stone of Indian legend: a stone that turns iron into gold just by touching it. Gurbani calls the Guru a paras, and Sikhs say the same of the sangat, the company of the good. You don't become gold by thinking about gold. You become gold by contact. Notice how practical that makes truth. It isn't mainly an argument you win. It's a substance you're near, or not. In Sikh life, one way people stay near it is small, repeated faithfulness: the morning banis, said every day; the word kept; the promise honored when it's inconvenient. Every kept promise is a little contact with the true. That's why today's practice is so small. In this picture, nobody becomes true in one heroic act. It happens the way iron becomes gold in the old story: touch by touch.
screen: `TRUE THING, TRUE PERSON: EACH LINE.` · `BHAGAT: THE DEVOTEE.` · `PARAS: IRON TURNED TO GOLD.` · `A KEPT PROMISE IS CONTACT.` · then, large: `BECOME TRUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one promise to keep. Sit and think back over the week: something you said you'd do and haven't yet. A call, a returned book, a 'let's get coffee' you didn't mean. Pick one that's small enough to do today. Picture yourself keeping it, simply, without announcing it. Treat it as a kind of touch, contact with what's true. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you decide. The bell holds the time.
Paras, the legendary stone that turns iron to gold. The bhagat becomes true by touching the true, like iron turned to gold: touch by touch.
Your line: become true. Keep one promise today, even a tiny one, and keep it quietly. Day five hundred four.

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's seventeenth ashtpadi hear each true thing paired with the person who meets it, and Gurbani calls the Guru a paras, the stone that turns iron to gold.

fork.setup: you want to become a more truthful person. by the seventeenth ashtpadi, what's the way in?
options: small, repeated contact with the true, like keeping promises.
fork.reveal: touch by touch, like iron near the paras. each kept promise is a little contact with what's true.

original.note: Gurmukhi: paras, the legendary stone that turns iron to gold; Gurbani uses it for the Guru.

trapdoor: what you thought: devotees are true because they're especially holy.
what it means: they become true by contact with the true, touch by touch.
what a scholar hears: the stanza ends bujhanhaar kau sat sabh hoi, for the one who understands all becomes true; the paras image recurs across Gurbani and Bhai Gurdas.

Editor review (2026-10-01): softened 'often called a paras' and 'the main way' to claims the text supports; the becoming-true line is framed as the stanza's picture; practice no longer tells the listener what to feel. Keeper: give an Ang for the Guru as paras (e.g. gur paaras ham loh).
